title: Classic Poutine Feed for the Crew
displayTitle: Classic Poutine Feed for the Crew
seoTitle: Classic Poutine Feed for the Crew | Firefighter Meal
shortDescription: Double-fried fries with beef gravy and cheese curds for ten
subtitle: Double-fried fries with beef gravy and cheese curds for ten
description: Russet potatoes are cut thick, fried twice until shatter-crisp, then topped with hot beef gravy and squeaky cheese curds. Serve immediately on platters because poutine waits for no one—not even the captain.

steps.title: Gather ingredients and equipment
steps.instruction: Line up every ingredient for Classic Poutine Feed for the Crew in the order you will cook — measure spices into ramekins, trim proteins on a dedicated board, and set tongs, thermometers, and hotel pans within arm's reach before any heat goes on.

steps.title: Preheat ovens and surfaces
steps.instruction: Preheat ovens, griddles, or grills to recipe temp before the crew arrives — cold equipment extends cook time and dries out batch beef. Confirm burners ignite evenly and sheet pans are greased or lined.

steps.title: Cut and soak fries
steps.instruction: Cut potatoes into thick fries, soak in cold water 30 minutes, then drain and dry completely on towels. Work in batches if the pan or grill crowding steams food instead of browning — rookies should watch for pale surfaces and adjust heat early.

steps.title: First fry
steps.instruction: Blanch fries in 325°F oil 4–5 minutes until soft but not browned. Drain, cool on racks at least 20 minutes. Target oven/smoker temperature: 325°F.

steps.title: Build beef gravy
steps.instruction: Melt drippings, whisk in flour, cook 2 minutes, then whisk in broth, Worcestershire, and garlic powder. Simmer until thick enough to coat a spoon.

steps.title: Second fry
steps.instruction: Fry blanched potatoes at 375°F until deep golden and crisp, 3–4 minutes. Drain, salt immediately. Target oven/smoker temperature: 375°F.

steps.title: Verify safe internal temps
steps.instruction: Spot-check the thickest pieces with an instant-read thermometer — target 145°F for medium beef, 160°F for ground. If any piece reads low, return it to heat immediately rather than holding under temp on the line.

steps.title: Hold for call interruptions
steps.instruction: If tones drop mid-service, cover finished food and hold at 140°F in a warm cabinet or 200°F oven — never leave proteins below 140°F for more than 30 minutes cumulative. Note the hold time on the pan with a grease pencil.

steps.title: Portion and open the line
steps.instruction: Portion Classic Poutine Feed for the Crew onto sheet trays or hotel pans for family-style service. Stack plates, forks, and napkins at the end of the line so late-arriving crew can self-serve without bottlenecking the cook.

steps.title: Scale for larger halls
steps.instruction: When cooking for more than 10 firefighters, split into two pans halfway through so the bottom layer does not overcook while the top waits — duplicate mise en place if you double batches.

steps.title: Assemble and serve
steps.instruction: Pile hot fries on platters, scatter curds, ladle hot gravy over top, and serve at once with pepper mills on the table. Plan about 5 minutes for this step at crew scale. Keep a backup tray at 200°F for firefighters returning from a call — never serve picked-over pans to late crew. Work in batches if the pan or grill crowding steams food instead of browning — rookies should watch for pale surfaces and adjust heat early.

proTips: If curds are unavailable, use whole-milk mozzarella torn into chunks—never pre-shredded.
A splash of apple cider vinegar in gravy adds Quebec-style tang.
Vent the fryer area—poutine night smokes up the hall fast.
tonightSpread: Classic poutine platters with extra gravy on the side.
Simple vinegar coleslaw to cut the richness between bites.
leftovers: Honestly? Leftover poutine is a lost cause—plan portions tight.
Save gravy for hot beef sandwiches the next shift.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Poutine is the ultimate Canadian hall comfort food. Crisp fries, rich gravy, and melting curds hit every craving after a cold call. This is the real deal—no poached eggs, no pulled pork gimmicks.
mealPrepNotes: Par-fry potatoes earlier in the day and finish-fry at service. Gravy must be hot enough to soften curds but not so hot it breaks them to mush. Work in batches so fries stay crisp.
